title: Salience Network Changes
subtitle: Selecting what deserves attention now
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating salience network changes across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain salience network changes in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in salience network changes.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to salience network changes.

sections.explainSimply: The salience network helps detect important internal and external events and switch between modes of processing.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Trauma can bias attention toward threat cues and bodily signals, increasing rapid switching into defensive states.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Anterior insula and dorsal anterior cingulate are central nodes, but network findings are not specific enough for diagnosis.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of salience network changes as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need salience network changes to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Do not treat connectivity maps as direct readouts of symptoms.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use salience network changes to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses salience network changes to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Do not treat connectivity maps as direct readouts of symptoms. Evidence classification: promising network evidence.
